newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JAN 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JAN 13.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Major changes, signalled by the sale of the Bank of Attica, are on the cards for the banking scene. Priorities for the government are modernisation of state-run banks which hold the lion's share of the market and assistance for private banks dealing with intensified competition. The basis for dialogue between government and banks will be the report on the size, prospects and problems of the banking system and proposals for its reorganisation, to be handed to National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou today or tomorrow.
--Twenty-five public works projects worth a total of 300 billion drachmas will be tendered in the first months of 1997, giving the construction industry a sound start to the new year.

--Closer Greek-Russian cooperation in the energy sector and particularly the fields of natural gas and petroleum will be the focus of discussions today between the Russian energy minister and Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
--Mutual funds with fixed returns have seen significant inflows: the taxation of state titles and the reforms to the taxation of mutual funds has given handling companies the comparitive advantage.

--The audit by international financial houses conducted on Athens bourse members and listed companies has revealed fictitious transactions by three listed companies aimed at receiving indirect funding from the capital market, and driving up the price of their shares. The Capital Market Commission meanwhile is expected to impose sanctions later in the week.
--Deputy Finance Minister George Drys has ordered a committee to look into reducing fines for non-payment of Value Added Tax in an effort to recoup at least some of the revenues.

--The first meeting of the Agricultural Policy Council failed to provide any answers to the issues facing Greek agriculture as the opposition restricted itself to a criticism of the government for indifference and farmers' representatives showed they were out of touch with the base.

--Greek-Turkish trade is at particularly low levels - 410 million dollars in 1995 - despite an upward trend and margins for growth. Many stress that better trade relations would have a run-off effect on political relations.

--Thirty-three major state enterprises will see new hands at the wheel in the course of 1997 as the national economy ministry has already begun work on plans to place private sector managers and trimmed-back boards of directors in state-run organisations.
--Along with the beginning of dialogue of farming issues, a memorandum will be addressed to the European Commission on the granting of Community funds for farmers whose crops have been damaged.

--The National Bank of Greece is examining the prospect of granting shares to staff in an effort to keep wage increases under projected inflation and whether it will be possible to distribute shares rather than dividends to stock holders this year.

--The fall in drachma interest rates will lead to placings designed to ensure the best results for investment capital. The outlook is good, given the drachma remains in a strong position: however, the reports of the current accounts balance deficit exceeding 4.5 billion dollars are worrying. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
